children: By Jamie Waters
Kedric Walker Jr. thought he was in for a "cute little workout."
He was joining his wife, Sabrina Walker, for a class at Solidcore, a trendy chain where fitness buffs sweat it out on Pilates-inspired reformer machines.

Then the doors closed and "the instructor started yelling at me like we were at an auction," said Kedric, a full-time firefighter and a CrossFit regular in Birmingham, Ala. All around him, women half his size were "rocking it." An hour later, he emerged tired and hungry, his legs shaking like a Chihuahua's.

Sabrina, the owner of a real-estate business, documented his anguish in a TikTok video that has received more than three million likes since August. "How you feel, boo? Are you crying?" she asks in the video. After he tells her he's just hungry, they get lunch, where Kedric, 32, prays that the Lord will "heal us from Pilates."

Boyfriends and husbands are learning the hard way that their female companions are not going to 7 a.m. classes just to stretch. Gym bros accustomed to bench-presses and burpees swagger into serene studios expecting to spend 50 minutes doing light exercises with toy dumbbells. Many severely underestimate the difficulty of Pilates or its high-intensity offshoots, which are built on low-impact movements that prioritize core strength, posture and slow burn. They leave broken men-much to their partners' delight.

Though women continue to dominate the discipline, more men are participating. The number of men doing Pilates at Life Time's roughly 200 athletic clubs in North America, for instance, has more than doubled over the past five years. Some guys become interested after seeing videos of NFL players gliding on reformers during the off-season. Many are introduced by the women in their lives.

"All the girls want to bring their boyfriends and husbands," said Laura Wilson, founder of Natural Pilates, a studio in Los Angeles and New York. She said women typically bring their partners after the partners say: "'What is this 'Pilates' and why is it so expensive?'"
Usually, she said, the women tell their instructors: "Make sure you kill them."

In Wilson's early-morning classes in Beverly Hills, West Hollywood and Sherman Oaks, three or four of the 13 reformers are claimed by men, she said-a 25% increase from a couple of years ago. More of the guys are younger now, said Wilson. The vast majority first came with a female companion.

She said certain Pilates moves can be more difficult for men. "Their legs are like three times heavier than women's, so when they do an exercise where their legs are out on a diagonal, they need to exert three times more force." Though Pilates is a full-body workout, she added, it often focuses on glutes and legs, which many men neglect in their gym workouts.

Like the men I spoke to, I'd never done Pilates before. But I'm a HIIT class regular and a keen runner, so I figured I would do alright. One recent weekend I headed to reformer Pilates with my sister. Ten minutes and a flutter of scissor kicks later, my thighs felt like concrete pylons, and my hip flexors, which I was previously unacquainted with, were screaming.

Then, while trying to put my feet into these stirrup things like I was about to give birth, I fell off the machine. My sister nearly coughed up a lung from laughing, though, like any self-respecting Pilates princess, she didn't break form. (After class, I watched an Instagram video of NFL wide receiver Stefon Diggs falling off a reformer, which cheered me up immensely.)
The toughest part? Unlike my HIIT workouts, the handful of Pilates classes I attended didn't allow any breaks. In one, the "reset" between exercises was an ab plank. That is not a reset!

The relentless burn also wiped the smile off the face of Josué Loza, a delivery driver who accompanied his girlfriend, Karen Escandon, to a hot Pilates class in Houston several months ago. A before-and-after video that Escandon, a housecleaner, posted to TikTok received more than 135,000 "likes."

Loza, 26, is "used to throwing weights around," and at the start of the mat Pilates class, which was held in a 100-degree studio, he asked Escandon if the dumbbells would seriously only be 2.5 pounds. "He was talking so much crap," said Escandon.

Within 10 minutes, he was drenched with sweat and out of breath. "The instructor kept telling me, 'Hey, proper form, proper form, proper form,' and I was like, 'Ma'am, I can't even lift my legs,'" said Loza.
His soul, he said, left his body.

Though Loza hasn't returned to Pilates-"I can't show my face in there again"-the experience made him reassess his physicality. His ability to hurl 500-pound dumbbells means nothing, he said, if he can't execute simple bodyweight movements. Loza has since changed his gym routine to focus more on building flexibility.
"I don't power lift anymore," he said. "I am a new man."
